articles.headline: S&P 500 barely moves, but more stocks are gaining ground
articles.dek: The index closed almost flat, but more stocks rose than fell for a fourth straight day. Strategists say that's a healthier sign than the flat number suggests.
articles.body:
The S&P 500 closed nearly unchanged today. But look past that number, and the market showed real strength underneath.

More stocks rose than fell today, the widest gain in almost three weeks. Mid-size industrial companies and regional banks led the way, while the biggest technology stocks took a breather after recent gains.

Strategists see this as a healthy shift, not a warning sign. Investors are moving money out of the most crowded trades and into stocks that had lagged since spring. That kind of rebalancing has usually come before further gains, not a market top.

The next big test arrives with next week's inflation report. It will help determine whether the Federal Reserve sticks with its expected pace of interest rate cuts, or whether investors need to brace for fewer cuts than they currently expect.
articles.author: M. Halvorsen
articles.theoryBody:
Graduate treatments of inflation dynamics typically start from a New Keynesian Phillips curve, where current inflation is pinned down by expected future inflation plus a term reflecting the output gap or real marginal cost, rather than by past inflation alone. Because expectations of future inflation do most of the work in this framework, asset prices can move well ahead of any given data release: investors are effectively pricing in the inflation path implied by current output and labor market slack, then revising that path as new information arrives.

The breadth improvement described in this piece is consistent with that logic. If market participants believe underlying price pressure is being contained without a demand-side hard landing, both cyclical and previously lagging sectors can re-rate together, since the same expected inflation path feeds into the discount rate applied across the index rather than into a handful of names.

The risk to this reading sits in the same equation: because current pricing already embeds an expected inflation path, a data surprise does not just update the current inflation number, it forces a repricing of the entire expected path going forward, which is why single data releases can move markets by more than the surprise in the number alone would suggest.

articles.headline: Options traders are betting on a calmer market into month end
articles.dek: A key measure of expected stock-market swings has dropped to its lowest level since January, and trading patterns suggest calm conditions may continue.
articles.body:
This deeper dive is available to Plus and Pro members.

Options traders are betting on calm markets. Positioning data shows market makers are set up to buy dips and sell rallies to stay balanced -- a routine hedging pattern, not a market call. That kind of automatic buying and selling smooths out price swings, which explains why the index has traded in such a tight range over the past two weeks.

Our take: unless growth or inflation data delivers a real surprise, expect the market to drift rather than move sharply in either direction, at least until options tied to the current expiration date are settled.
articles.author: M. Halvorsen

articles.headline: Chip stocks split: AI winners rise while others fall behind
articles.dek: Semiconductor makers tied to AI chips are outperforming, while more diversified chipmakers lag, even though the sector's overall index barely moved this week.
articles.body:
The semiconductor index closed the week almost exactly where it started. But that flat number hides a real split underneath.

Companies making chips for AI systems keep getting more optimistic forecasts from analysts. Meanwhile, chipmakers that also sell to consumer electronics and older technology are falling behind.

This split is becoming one of the defining stories of this earnings season. Investors increasingly want exposure to companies clearly tied to data center growth. They're willing to pay less for chipmakers without that connection, even if those companies are otherwise well-run.
articles.author: J. Lindqvist
articles.theoryBody:
Schumpeterian growth theory, formalized in modern endogenous growth models, treats a wave of innovation not as a rising tide that lifts an entire sector, but as a process that reallocates capital and market share away from incumbents toward whichever firms hold the frontier technology at a given moment. Divergence within an industry index, rather than a uniform re-rating, is the signature this theory predicts when a genuine technological shift, rather than a cyclical demand swing, is underway.

The semiconductor split described in this piece is a fairly clean example: capital is not leaving the sector, it is being reallocated within it toward the firms positioned at the current technological frontier, which the theory would treat as an efficient, if uncomfortable for laggards, response to a real shift in the expected return on capital across different parts of the value chain.

articles.headline: Three scenarios for data center spending next year
articles.dek: Our base, bull, and bear cases for how much big tech companies will spend on AI infrastructure, and what each outcome means for chipmakers and suppliers.
articles.body:
This is a dedicated analyst note, available to Pro members.

We built three scenarios for how much the largest cloud computing companies will spend on data centers over the next year. Our estimates come from public company guidance, historical spending patterns, and lead-time data from equipment suppliers.

In our base case, spending keeps growing at a slower but still strong double-digit pace, as the biggest cloud providers absorb equipment they've already ordered. Our bull case assumes spending accelerates further as more businesses adopt AI tools faster than expected. Our bear case models a pause, as public investors start demanding clearer proof this spending is paying off.

We map out what each scenario means for equipment makers, memory chip prices, and power infrastructure companies, along with how we'd size positions in each.
articles.author: J. Lindqvist
articles.theoryBody:
Two complementary frameworks anchor most graduate treatments of corporate investment. Tobin's Q relates investment to the ratio of a firm's market valuation to the replacement cost of its capital: when Q is comfortably above one, the theory predicts firms should keep adding capital because financial markets are valuing that capital above what it costs to build. The accelerator model instead ties investment more mechanically to the expected growth rate of demand, treating capex as a derived response to the pace at which capacity needs to expand.

The three scenarios modeled in this note map fairly directly onto both lenses: the bull case is consistent with persistently high Q sustaining capex even as growth moderates, the base case reflects an accelerator-style deceleration as the rate of demand growth, not its level, slows, and the bear case models a scenario where public-market scrutiny compresses Q enough that even firms with strong underlying demand pull back on planned capital spending.

articles.headline: Fed official signals openness to a rate cut by December
articles.dek: A Federal Reserve governor said the central bank could cut interest rates by year-end if inflation keeps cooling. Treasury yields fell on the news.
articles.body:
A Federal Reserve governor said today the central bank could cut interest rates before year-end if inflation data keeps improving. It was the clearest signal yet from a voting member about the Fed's December meeting.

The governor made the remarks in a speech to a regional business group. Investors who track interest-rate expectations noticed an immediate shift: the tone was more open to cutting rates than the Fed's messaging after its last meeting. The governor didn't commit to a specific move, but investors read the comments as a signal that a cut is now more likely.

The 2-year Treasury yield, which tends to move with interest-rate expectations, fell 5 basis points -- meaning bond prices rose slightly as investors bet borrowing costs will come down. Futures markets nudged up the odds of a December rate cut, and the S&P 500 closed modestly higher.

This matters because it narrows the gap between what the Fed is signaling and what investors already expected. If inflation reports due before the next two meetings come in soft, today's comments give the Fed room to cut rates without surprising markets. If inflation surprises to the upside instead, today's comments will look premature.

Fed Watch take: the next two inflation reports now carry more weight for the December decision than today's speech itself.
articles.author: R. Costa

articles.headline: Strong jobs report puts a rate hike back on the table
articles.dek: August hiring came in far above expectations, undercutting hopes for a rate cut after a Fed governor's comments earlier in the week.
articles.body:
Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said Thursday the Fed could hold interest rates steady this month if inflation data continued to improve. He added the Fed would raise rates instead if inflation ran hot.

A day later, the government's August jobs report told a different story. Employers added 162,000 jobs last month, more than triple the roughly 53,000 economists expected. Unemployment held steady at 4.1%, and hiring figures from June and July were revised higher.

U.S. markets are closed today for Labor Day, but Friday's trading captured the shift. The Dow fell 271.86 points, the S&P 500 slipped 0.38% to 7,718.60, and the 2-year Treasury yield -- a rate that moves closely with Fed policy expectations -- rose to 4.377%, its highest level since January 2025. Investors tracking Fed futures now see roughly 60% odds of a quarter-point rate hike at the September 15-16 meeting, up sharply from earlier in the week.

This puts enormous weight on next week's inflation reports, the last major data before the Fed meets. Waller has said his vote depends on whether inflation kept improving in August. A hot reading would likely push him, and possibly other officials, toward raising rates instead of holding steady.

Fed Watch take: strong hiring just made holding rates steady less likely. Next week's inflation data now looks more likely to decide between a hike and a hold than between holding and cutting.
articles.author: R. Costa

articles.headline: Rate-hike odds cool slightly, but a decision remains a coin flip
articles.dek: With no new economic data over the long weekend, prediction markets did the moving. Betting markets now put a quarter-point September hike at 49%, down from Friday's spike.
articles.body:
No new economic data came out over the Labor Day weekend, but prediction markets kept shifting anyway. Betting platform Polymarket's contract on the Fed's September decision now shows a 52% chance the Fed holds rates steady, and a 49% chance it raises them a quarter point. That's down from the sharper bets on a hike seen right after Friday's strong August jobs report.

Stock and bond markets are closed today for Labor Day, so Friday's closing prices are still the latest hard numbers: the 2-year Treasury yield at 4.377% and the 10-year at 4.784%, both up for the week. The Fed's benchmark interest rate has held between 3.50% and 3.75% since its July meeting.

This near-even split reflects real disagreement inside the Fed. Officials themselves split 9-3 at their July meeting, with three members wanting an immediate rate hike. Governor Waller has said his own vote depends specifically on whether August inflation data kept improving the way July's did. Next week's inflation reports are the last major data before officials vote.

Fed Watch take: the gap between holding rates and raising them is now smaller than the market's usual noise this close to a decision. A single soft or hot inflation report next week could tip the outcome either way.
articles.author: R. Costa

articles.headline: Bond yields rise as investors brace for a big week of inflation data
articles.dek: The 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 4.81%, and betting markets still see roughly 58% odds of a rate hike, as investors await this week's inflation reports.
articles.body:
Treasury yields rose again today as markets reopened after the holiday weekend. Rising energy costs and an upcoming wave of inflation data pushed the 10-year Treasury yield -- a benchmark that influences mortgage rates and corporate borrowing costs -- up more than 2 basis points to 4.81%. The 2-year yield held roughly flat at 4.38%, while the 30-year climbed to 5.27%.

Betting markets still show roughly 58% odds of a quarter-point interest-rate hike at the Fed's September 15-16 meeting, little changed from Friday. Oil prices also rose Monday, adding another reason for investors to worry about inflation.

Investors are now focused on this week's wholesale inflation report and Wednesday's consumer inflation report, the last major data before the Fed meets. Comments from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh last month, which raised the possibility of a rate hike, remain the hawkish benchmark investors are measuring new data against.

Fed Watch take: with rate-hike odds already high and mostly priced in, this week's inflation reports carry unusual power to either confirm the case for a hike or reopen the debate about holding steady.
articles.author: R. Costa

articles.headline: Yen strengthens as investors bet on a Bank of Japan rate hike
articles.dek: Japan's Nikkei index hit a fresh high even as the yen strengthened, with investors increasingly confident the central bank will raise rates this month.
articles.body:
Japan's currency strengthened Tuesday as Asian markets traded without a clear direction. The move came a day after the Nikkei 225 stock index jumped 2.12% to close at 66,400, its second straight day of gains led by technology stocks. The index touched a fresh high near 66,525 Tuesday morning in Tokyo.

The stronger yen comes as investors grow more confident the Bank of Japan will raise interest rates at its meeting this month. That confidence is built on July wage growth running at its fastest pace since 1997, and an upward revision to economic growth figures for the spring. A stronger yen typically hurts Japan's export-heavy companies, since it makes their products more expensive for foreign buyers, even as it lowers the cost of imported goods.

Monday's stock rally was driven by chipmakers and AI-related companies -- Kioxia, SoftBank, and Advantest all posted strong gains -- on optimism that a rumored new AI model from OpenAI could boost demand for Japanese semiconductor equipment. Financial and consumer companies lagged behind.

What to watch: the Bank of Japan's policy decision this month, and how a strengthening yen interacts with rising oil prices tied to the ongoing Middle East conflict. Together, those two forces could pull Japan's inflation outlook in different directions.
articles.author: S. Okafor

articles.headline: Taiwan's stock index nears a record as MediaTek surges on Nvidia deal
articles.dek: Taiwan's benchmark index climbed 1.9% toward its June record. Chipmaker MediaTek jumped after Nvidia invested $3.5 billion in the company's bond offering.
articles.body:
Taiwan's benchmark TAIEX index climbed 863 points, or 1.9%, to 47,414 in Monday trading, moving back toward the record it set in June. The gains were broad, with the electronics-heavy technology segment of the index up 2.3% on bets that memory chip demand will strengthen, tied to rumors of a new AI model from OpenAI.

Chipmaker MediaTek stood out, surging as much as 9.7% after Nvidia agreed to invest $3.5 billion in the company's record $3.9 billion overseas bond offering -- a deal that also deepens the two companies' business ties. TSMC, which makes up more than 40% of the index's total value, rose roughly 2%. Chip-testing company ASE Technology jumped 5.3%.

Investors are now watching Taiwan's August trade data, due later this week, for a clearer sign of whether AI-driven chip demand is showing up in real export numbers, not just rising stock prices.

What to watch: whether the trade data confirms strong AI-related demand, and how investors react to TSMC's plans to significantly increase spending on new factories in 2026 and 2027 once the company reports third-quarter results.
articles.author: J. Lindqvist

articles.headline: Vietnam's major stock market upgrade is two weeks away
articles.dek: Index provider FTSE Russell will officially upgrade Vietnam to emerging-market status on September 21, capping an eight-year process and opening the door to new foreign investment.
articles.body:
Vietnam is entering the final stretch before a milestone for its stock market. Index provider FTSE Russell will officially reclassify the country from frontier-market to secondary emerging-market status on September 21, just under two weeks from now. The upgrade caps an eight-year process that began when Vietnam first joined FTSE's watchlist in 2018.

The reclassification places Vietnam alongside China, India, Indonesia, and the Philippines in FTSE's market rankings. It should also trigger new investment from large funds that automatically buy stocks based on these rankings, as Vietnamese companies join FTSE's benchmark index over the next year. Vietnam's VN-Index has already climbed sharply in anticipation, roughly doubling in value since April 2025.

One key reform made this possible: Vietnam removed a rule that once forced foreign investors to fund stock trades in advance, before knowing if their orders would be filled. That rule was long considered the biggest obstacle keeping large institutional investors out of Vietnamese stocks.

What to watch: with much of the good news already reflected in stock prices, some analysts expect a short-term pullback once the upgrade actually takes effect on September 21, even though the longer-term case for sustained foreign investment remains strong.
articles.author: N. Suwannarat

articles.headline: Intel shares jump on planned price hikes and a manufacturing milestone
articles.dek: Intel stock rose as much as 5% after reports the company plans to raise PC chip prices, alongside a Wall Street upgrade and news of a manufacturing breakthrough.
articles.body:
Intel shares jumped as much as 5.4% Tuesday, extending last week's rally, after industry sources told trade publication DigiTimes the company plans to raise prices on PC processors by roughly 10% starting in October. Separately, Wall Street firm Northland upgraded Intel's stock rating, citing signs of a business turnaround and reported shortages of server chips.

The rally also followed a manufacturing milestone: Intel's factory division and equipment maker ASML said they've now produced more than one million silicon wafers using a new, more precise chipmaking technology. That same technology is also being adopted by rivals Samsung and TSMC. Nvidia's roughly $30 billion investment in Intel continues to reassure investors that the company's turnaround is on track.

Intel's gains stood out against a weaker overall market -- the S&P 500 and the tech-heavy Nasdaq index both slipped slightly Tuesday -- showing the rally was driven by Intel-specific news rather than the broader sector.

What to watch: whether the October price increases go over well with computer makers, who are already navigating a slow period for PC sales, and further details on Intel's advanced manufacturing capacity as it competes for AI-related business.
articles.author: J. Lindqvist

articles.headline: Treasury boosts bond buybacks, pushing long-term rates to a three-year high
articles.dek: Treasury Secretary Bessent tripled the government's bond buyback program to steady the bond market, but long-term interest rates rose anyway, adding to the case for a Fed rate hike.
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced Wednesday that the government will triple its buyback of long-term government bonds to $6 billion, up from the $2 billion initially announced last month. The move -- essentially buying back existing government debt to support prices -- aims to steady a bond market that's been under pressure from rising interest rates. It follows an August 19 pledge to at least double the buyback program, and comes as oil prices keep climbing toward $100 a barrel.

The announcement had the opposite of its intended effect. The 10-year Treasury yield, a benchmark that influences mortgage rates and corporate borrowing costs, jumped to 4.857%, its highest level since November 2023. The 2-year yield held near 4.39%. Stocks fell alongside the move, with the Dow dropping 333 points, the S&P 500 losing 0.4%, and the Nasdaq down 0.5%.

Betting markets now show roughly 58% odds of a quarter-point interest-rate hike at next week's Fed meeting, up from about 52% after Friday's strong jobs report. Rising bond yields and oil prices are both adding pressure toward that outcome, just as Fed officials prepare to decide.

Fed Watch take: if oil keeps climbing toward $100 a barrel, it becomes harder for Fed officials who favor holding rates steady to make their case.
articles.author: R. Costa

articles.headline: Yen hits seven-month high, pressuring Japan's exporters
articles.dek: Treasury Secretary Bessent's comments about Japan's currency policy sent the yen higher Wednesday, hurting exporter stocks even as chipmakers held steady.
articles.body:
Japan's Nikkei 225 stock index slipped 0.19% Wednesday to close at 65,143, giving back an early gain. The broader TOPIX index eased 0.09% to 4,046.64. The declines came after Japan's currency strengthened to its highest level in nearly seven months, with the dollar falling to around 153.63 yen. The move followed comments from U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who said he has close insight into the Bank of Japan's efforts to support the yen and warned investors against betting the currency will weaken further.

A stronger yen directly hurts Japan's export-heavy companies, since it makes their products more expensive for foreign buyers. Video game maker Nintendo dropped 4%, clothing retailer Fast Retailing fell 2.7%, chip-equipment maker Advantest lost 2.8%, and Mitsubishi UFJ bank slid 1.5%. Semiconductor and AI-related stocks held up better. Rising oil prices, approaching $100 a barrel, added to inflation concerns and kept expectations for a Bank of Japan rate hike alive.

What to watch: the Bank of Japan's next policy meeting. Hawkish signals from advisers close to Prime Minister Takaichi, plus the fastest wage growth since 1997, have fueled speculation of a September rate hike. A further rise in the yen would add even more pressure on exporters heading into earnings season.
articles.author: S. Okafor

articles.headline: Taiwan's stock index edges higher as investors take profits on TSMC
articles.dek: Shares gave back early gains as investors grew cautious on chipmaker TSMC ahead of this week's U.S. inflation data.
articles.body:
Taiwan's TAIEX index closed up 77.58 points, or 0.16%, at 47,183.36 on Wednesday, after swinging between 47,060.78 and 47,548.26 during the session. TSMC, which makes up more than 40% of the index's total value, fell 0.20% to NT$2,465.00, down from an earlier high of NT$2,490.00, as investors sold shares to lock in gains after the company's U.S.-listed shares had jumped 2.35% overnight.

The rally stalled as the index approached its June record high near 48,200, with traders citing caution ahead of this week's U.S. consumer inflation report. TSMC's supply-chain partners stayed in focus after the company and equipment maker ASML said they're adopting a larger, more advanced photomask format used in chipmaking, and after ASML confirmed new equipment orders from both TSMC and Samsung tied to AI-related demand.

What to watch: Taiwan's August export order data, a closely watched signal of global chip demand, along with how this week's U.S. inflation report affects expectations for American interest rates.
articles.author: J. Lindqvist

articles.headline: Vietnam's stock index slips as smaller companies offset an early oil-driven rally
articles.dek: Vietnam's benchmark index gave back early gains built on rising oil prices, as declines in small and mid-size stocks pulled the market lower.
articles.body:
Vietnam's VN-Index fell 0.18% to close at 1,827.12 points on Wednesday, giving back an early gain that had been driven by rising global oil prices lifting energy stocks. Morning leaders GAS (+1.54%) and BSR (+1.30%) faded as investors took profits, and the index turned negative in the afternoon on broad weakness among small and mid-size stocks, led by property developers Vinhomes (down 2.04%) and Vingroup (down 0.76%).

More stocks fell than rose, with 190 decliners against 120 gainers. Foreign investors were net sellers of 270.8 billion Vietnamese dong, while total trading volume rose 2.8% from the prior session, suggesting the pullback drew active buying and selling rather than a quiet drift lower.

What to watch: whether rising oil prices keep supporting energy stocks even as the broader market digests recent gains, and how expectations for U.S. interest rates affect Vietnam's currency -- a factor worth watching closely, with the country's major stock-index upgrade just under two weeks away.
articles.author: N. Suwannarat

articles.headline: AMD jumps 3% as its finance chief raises AI chip sales forecast to $3 trillion
articles.dek: Chip stocks bucked a broader tech pullback after AMD's finance chief said demand for AI chips is outpacing the company's own earlier projections.
articles.body:
AMD shares rose about 3% Wednesday after Chief Financial Officer Jean Hu said the company now expects the total market for AI chips to approach $3 trillion, above the estimate AMD gave when it first outlined the opportunity. Hu said demand from major customers including Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic has come in stronger than AMD expected when it struck those partnerships. Intel shares also rose slightly on hopes for more manufacturing and packaging business.

The gains stood out against a weaker broader market: the tech-heavy Nasdaq index slipped as Treasury yields jumped to a three-year high, after the U.S. Treasury tripled its bond buyback program. AMD's revenue from data-center chips grew 107% from a year earlier to $6.72 billion last quarter, now 58% of the company's total sales -- a sign of how central AI infrastructure has become to its business. Hu also confirmed TSMC remains AMD's main manufacturing partner.

What to watch: confirmation of the higher sales forecast at AMD's next investor update, and upcoming earnings from Nvidia and Broadcom for signs of whether big tech companies keep raising their own AI spending plans.
articles.author: J. Lindqvist

articles.headline: Bond yields ease as investors await Friday's inflation report
articles.dek: The 10-year Treasury yield dipped slightly after hitting a three-year high, with investors now focused on the last inflation data before next week's Fed decision.
articles.body:
The 10-year Treasury yield eased to 4.84% Thursday, a hair below Wednesday's 4.85% close -- itself the highest level since October 2023 -- as markets absorbed this week's tripled government bond buyback. The 2-year yield held near 4.40%, little changed.

Continued selling of U.S. Treasury bonds by Japan, as Tokyo works to support its currency, added further upward pressure on yields even as they eased slightly today. Betting markets still show roughly 58% odds of a quarter-point rate hike at next week's September 16 Fed meeting, matching Wednesday's reading.

Friday's August inflation report is the last major data point before the Fed meets, and investors are treating it as the deciding factor. A high reading would likely push rate-hike odds higher, while an in-line or lower reading would revive the case for the Fed holding rates steady.

Fed Watch take: with bond yields already near three-year highs, and companies issuing record amounts of debt to fund AI investments, we'd expect the Fed to lean toward raising rates rather than risk looking soft on inflation this close to its target.
articles.author: R. Costa

articles.headline: Nikkei recovers as cooling oil prices ease pressure on Japanese stocks
articles.dek: Japanese stocks edged higher Thursday as oil prices pulled back, offsetting continued yen strength, with the Bank of Japan's policy decision just over a week away.
articles.body:
Japan's Nikkei 225 index climbed 128.17 points, or 0.20%, to close at 65,270.95 Thursday, recovering modestly after Wednesday's pullback. A cooling in the recent oil-price rally gave Japan's exporters some relief. The yen held near 153.4 per dollar, still close to its strongest level in roughly seven months.

The stronger yen continues to hurt Japan's export-heavy companies, even as it lowers the cost of imported energy. Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, still trades above $100 a barrel amid tensions tied to the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil shipping route. The Bank of Japan is widely expected to raise its policy interest rate to 1.25% at next week's meeting, its highest level in roughly 31 years. That move would further narrow the interest-rate gap with the U.S. that has driven much of the yen's recent strength.

What to watch: Friday's U.S. inflation report and next week's Bank of Japan decision, the two biggest catalysts for the dollar-yen exchange rate. A rate hike from Japan paired with a hot U.S. inflation number could push the yen even higher, adding pressure on exporters like Toyota as they head into earnings season.
articles.author: S. Okafor

articles.headline: TSMC's August revenue jumps 53% to a record on AI chip demand
articles.dek: Taiwan Semiconductor posted record monthly sales of NT$514.8 billion, reinforcing strong AI-related demand even as Taiwan's stock index holds just below its record high.
articles.body:
TSMC reported August revenue of NT$514.8 billion, or about $16.35 billion, up 53.3% from a year earlier and a fresh monthly record. The company credited continued strong demand for AI accelerator chips and its most advanced manufacturing technology. The results extend a run of outsized growth that has TSMC on track to meet its raised 2026 revenue guidance of slightly above 40% growth.

The number lands as Taiwan's benchmark TAIEX index holds just below its June record near 48,200. TSMC alone makes up more than 40% of the index's total value, meaning the company's revenue trend works as a rough gauge for the broader market's AI-driven strength. The report also follows news this week that TSMC and equipment maker ASML are adopting a larger, more advanced photomask format to support the company's next round of factory expansion.

What to watch: Taiwan's broader August export data, due in the coming days, for signs of whether the strength in TSMC's own numbers is showing up economy-wide. Also watch TSMC's third-quarter earnings on October 15 for confirmation that its higher 2026-2027 spending plans are translating into profit, not just revenue growth.
articles.author: J. Lindqvist

articles.headline: Indonesia's stock market falls 1.19% as rising oil prices weigh on investors
articles.dek: Rising oil prices and expectations for higher U.S. interest rates pressured Jakarta stocks Thursday, with infrastructure, financial, and agriculture companies leading the decline.
articles.body:
Indonesia's IDX Composite index fell 1.19% at Thursday's close in Jakarta, as infrastructure, financial, and agriculture stocks led the decline. More stocks fell than rose, by a margin of 530 to 160. Crude oil for October delivery rose 0.6% to $96.63 a barrel, while the international Brent benchmark added 0.5% to $101.71, extending a run driven by ongoing tensions in the Middle East. Indonesia's currency, the rupiah, weakened 0.33% to 17,542.90 per dollar.

Higher oil prices are especially difficult for economies like Indonesia that import most of their energy, since the added cost feeds directly into inflation. That's a particular concern now, as regional central banks weigh their own interest-rate decisions alongside a Federal Reserve that increasingly looks likely to raise U.S. rates. Nearby markets fared better: Singapore's benchmark index held up comparatively well, supported by strength in bank and real estate stocks.

What to watch: whether Friday's U.S. inflation report adds to investor caution across the region, and any signal from Indonesia's central bank on how it plans to balance supporting its currency against supporting economic growth heading into the fourth quarter.
articles.author: N. Suwannarat

articles.headline: Intel closes at $106 as Nvidia-backed AI investment accelerates
articles.dek: Intel shares extended their rally to $106.24, building on this week's $20 billion stock sale and Nvidia's roughly $30 billion investment in the chipmaker.
articles.body:
Intel shares closed at $106.24 Wednesday, adding to Tuesday's 9.05% jump to $104.47. That earlier gain followed the company's $20 billion stock offering, priced at $95 a share, to fund AI and factory expansion. Nvidia's roughly $30 billion investment in Intel, announced alongside the stock sale, has reassured investors about Intel's role in the broader AI buildout.

The rally reflects growing confidence in Intel's manufacturing ambitions. SK Hynix is reportedly considering Intel's factories, alongside TSMC, to manufacture next-generation memory chips used in AI systems -- a potential vote of confidence in Intel's push into advanced chip packaging. That's true even though the stock offering is expected to reduce Intel's per-share profit by an estimated 4% to 5% in the near term, since more shares now share the same profits.

What to watch: whether Intel holds above the $97 level that technical analysts have flagged as a key support point, and whether Intel's factory division lands a confirmed customer win for next-generation memory chips in the coming weeks -- a bigger validation of the AI investment story than any single day's stock move.
articles.author: J. Lindqvist
